# Mirror and Hexagonality: an h layer is a mirror wall, a c layer an inversion centre (13 Nov 2026; queued 11 Nov, DICTO yes; lead 1 of studies/2026-11-13-swaps-and-fixed-points)

**Conclusion (13 Nov 2026): the link holds exactly at the level of layers and pieces, but it does not carry the Hexagonality Law. An h layer is a mirror of its neighbours, its site group (order 12) is generated by reflections, and its plane is a wall that no hole piece crosses. A c layer exchanges up and down only by inversion through its balls (its group's reflections generate only 6 of 12), and pieces straddle its plane at every sampled weight. Both are PROVED, and checked exactly on 23 stackings, 141 layers and 10 weights (10350 checks, 0 failures). The prediction "Janus pieces are cut exactly on h mirrors" is FALSE as stated: every piece next to an h layer is cut on it, Janus or not, and Janus pieces are cut at the gap mid-plane, which is no mirror. The Hexagonality Law needs locality and the Swap Rule, not the mirror. What the layer exchange adds is that the two Janus orientations have equal volume, V(c|h) = V(h|c), which gives #57's "mean of the parents" with the Swap Rule.**

Script `scripts/mirror_hex.py` (logs `data/mirrorhex-pilot.log`, `data/mirrorhex.log`; data `data/pilot.json`, `data/full.json`; first
full run `data/mirrorhex-run1.log`, see Faults). Ran on the compute node through the job gate (jobs mirrorhex-pilot: 14 s,
315 checks; mirrorhex: 377 s, 12 processes, 10350 checks, FINAL ok). **Exact rational arithmetic**: fractional coordinates in the
basis a1, a2 (60 degrees) and z, the rational metric of #57, and the exact power cells of the census engine
(`studies/2026-10-25-stackings/scripts/engine.py`, executed from its file, not retyped: floats only propose candidate corners, and every
corner is solved and tested exactly). Point sets are compared exactly, modulo the lattice.

## Question (open-work, 11 Nov, DICTO yes)
"Do the h layers of a close-packed stacking (ABA, reflection at B) correspond to Wythoff mirrors of its layer/rod group, and the
c layers (ABC) to an off-mirror exchange, as in the Mirror Law (#107)? Tie #66 Hexagonality Law to the Mirror Law." The swaps study
(LEAD 1) sharpened it: "list which faces lie on the mirror plane of an h layer; predict that Janus pieces are cut exactly on h mirrors
and never on c layers."

## Setting
Layer k is at height z_k. It is h if layers k-1 and k+1 sit on the same position, c otherwise (#57). The maps through layer k are:
- sigma_k, the horizontal mirror (a, b, z) -> (a, b, 2 z_k - z);
- iota_k, the inversion through a ball p of layer k;
- the mirror through the gap mid-plane (negative control).

Pieces are the power cells of the holes (#57: octahedral weight 0, tetrahedral weight lam). The near pieces of layer k are:
- the octahedral halves touching it: the bottom half of gap k and the top half of gap k-1, cut at the hole's plane;
- the two tetrahedral pieces nearest to it, which are whole by #57.

Weights tested: lam = -7/16, -5/12, -1/4, -3/16, -1/16, 1/300, 1/10, 1/4, 1/3, 5/16. These are two per stretch, the sample set of
#57's exact check. Stackings tested: ABC, AB, ABAC (4H), ABCACB (6H), ABACACBCB (Sm), ABCB, ABCBCACAB, ABABCBCAC and the 16 window
words of #57 (one coincides with another), 23 words in all, with 80 h layers and 61 c layers.

## Results

**Proposition 1 (the layer's exchange; PROVED, classical).** sigma_k maps layers k-1, k, k+1 onto themselves iff layer k is h. iota_k
does so iff layer k is c.
*Proof.* sigma_k sends layer k+1's position to height k-1 unchanged, so it works iff k-1 and k+1 share a position. In-plane, the point
reflection through a B site sends A to C (2B - C = A modulo the lattice), so iota_k works iff k-1 and k+1 sit on the two different
other positions. ∎

Checked on all 141 layers. sigma_k is a symmetry of the whole periodic stacking iff the word is a palindrome about layer k: 30 of the 80
h layers. The gap mid-plane mirror is never a symmetry (141 of 141, the negative control).

**Proposition 2 (Wythoff or not; PROVED by exhaustion of the 24 point operations of the hexagonal lattice).** The site group of a ball
in its three layers has order 12 in both cases.
- **h layer.** The site group is D3h, with 4 reflections (the layer mirror and 3 vertical mirrors). They generate all 12 elements, so
  it is a Coxeter group (A1 x A2) and the up-down exchange is one of its Wythoff mirrors.
- **c layer.** The site group is D3d, with 3 reflections, all vertical. They generate only C3v (order 6). The up-down exchange is -I,
  the inversion, which lies on no mirror. D3d is not a reflection group.

80 of 80 h layers and 61 of 61 c layers came out this way. This is the exact sense of "h layers are mirrors, c layers off-mirror
exchanges".

**Theorem 3 (the pieces; PROVED with #57, checked exactly).** At every weight of the walk:

(a) **The near pieces of an h layer** are exchanged by sigma_k. That is, the bottom octahedral half of gap k is the mirror image of
the top half of gap k-1, and likewise for the near tetrahedral pieces. **The near pieces of a c layer** are exchanged by iota_k and
not by sigma_k. Checked at all 141 layers x 10 weights wherever the pieces exist, both ways round (iota fails at h layers, sigma at c
layers).

(b) **No hole piece crosses the plane of an h layer**, so the plane is a wall made of piece faces.
*Proof.* By #57 the near pieces are those of the pure stacking of layer k's type at the same positions. For an h layer this is the
hcp stacking, of which sigma_k is a global symmetry. Suppose a piece of a hole off the plane had interior points on both sides. Then it
would have interior points on the plane, which sigma_k fixes, and these would also be interior to its mirror image, the piece of a
different hole. Two pieces cannot overlap. ∎
Checked on all 6 pieces of gaps k-1 and k at all 80 h layers x 10 weights: none crosses. The faces in the plane, per lattice cell
on each side, mirror-paired (checked):
- for lam up to 1/10: one octahedral face and one tetrahedral face;
- for lam = 1/4, 1/3, 5/16: the tetrahedral face alone; the octahedral piece then meets the plane in no face and no edge.

(c) **The plane of a c layer is crossed at every sampled weight.** For lam <= -3/16 the octahedral pieces of both gaps straddle it.
For lam >= -1/16 the near tetrahedral pieces do. No piece face and no piece edge lies in a c-layer plane at any sampled weight
(61 x 10, checked). This part is observed at the samples only, not proved for every weight.

(d) **Whole octahedral pieces.** sigma_k maps the whole pieces of gaps k-1 and k onto each other only for the windows hhh and chc.
iota_k does so only for ccc and hch. Elsewhere only the near halves match (#57's rule of halves: the far halves follow the far layers).

**Corollary 4 (what the exchange gives the Hexagonality Law).** Write V(t|t') for a piece over a t layer and under a t' layer, with
V(t|t') = Lo(t) + Up(t') (#57, #61). Theorem 3(a) gives Lo(t) congruent to Up(t) for both types: by a mirror for h, by an inversion
for c. Hence **V(c|h) = V(h|c)**: the two orientations of the Janus pieces have equal volume. With the Swap Rule this is
V(c|h) = V(h|c) = (V(c|c) + V(h|h))/2, #57's "mean of the two parents" (and the 5 of #61's 4 : 5 : 6).

The Hexagonality Law itself, that each kind of piece totals a straight line in the share h, rests on the two-layer locality and the
Swap Rule (#66, #84). It holds whatever exchanges up and down at a layer, mirror or inversion. So the mirror is not its cause. The c
<-> h swap of the Law is the swap "mirror wall <-> inversion centre crossed by pieces". It is the same split as the Mirror Law's "on
the mirrors / off them", but it adds no new linear law.

**Compared with the Mirror Law (#107).** In #107 the faces between like cells lie on mirrors, and the middle-bond faces between the
two end types leave them. Here, at an h layer the faces in the mirror plane are shared between a piece and its own mirror image (like
with like). At a c layer the up and down pieces are exchanged through a point and meet across the plane, not in it. The analogy is
exact at the level of "which exchange", but the stacking has no Wythoff polytope behind it. The h mirror is a Wythoff mirror of the
local site group (D3h) only, not of a group acting on the whole stacking unless the word is a palindrome there.

## Answer to the brief
- h layers <-> mirrors: YES, exactly (Propositions 1 and 2, Theorem 3(a, b)).
- c layers <-> off-mirror exchange: YES, the inversion through the layer's balls. The site group D3d is not generated by reflections.
- "Janus pieces cut exactly on h mirrors, never on c layers": FALSE as stated. Every near piece of an h layer is cut on it (Janus or
  not), and Janus pieces are cut at gap mid-planes. "Never on c layers" holds for faces: no piece face lies in a c-layer plane at any
  sampled weight.
- Tie to the Hexagonality Law: the exchange gives V(c|h) = V(h|c) (Corollary 4). The linear law does not come from the mirror.

## Controls (10350 checks, all ok)
- **Positive** (should pass, did):
  - hcp (AB): every layer a mirror, also globally;
  - fcc (ABC): every layer an inversion centre;
  - the 24 point operations are isometries of the metric;
  - mirror-paired face counts above and below every h layer.
- **Negative** (should fail, did):
  - the gap mid-plane mirror is never a symmetry of the balls, and never maps a gap's two tetrahedral pieces onto each other
    (141 x 10);
  - sigma_k fails on every c layer and iota_k on every h layer, for the balls and for the near pieces;
  - the global mirror fails on the 50 h layers about which the word is not a palindrome.

## Faults fixed on the way
- Pilot: a Fraction used as a string index (site group). Fixed and rerun.
- First full run (`data/mirrorhex-run1.log`): the face census of the layer plane did not shift the faces of gap n-1 when layer 0 was
  tested. The census showed 2 instead of 4 faces at 15 h layers, all at k = 0, while corners and edges were shifted correctly. Fixed,
  then a check was added that face counts above and below a layer agree. The rerun (`data/mirrorhex.log`) is the one reported. The
  crossing and mapping checks were unaffected.

## LEADS
1. Prove Theorem 3(c) for every weight: a c-layer plane is crossed by some piece along the whole walk. The switch from octahedral to
   tetrahedral crossing lies between -3/16 and -1/16; find it exactly (expected near -1/8, a stop of the cubic walk).
2. Squashed layers (#61, spacing s < 1): there the near tetrahedral pieces are Ganesha (head and body from different layers). Does the
   h-layer wall survive? The mirror argument needs only Theorem 3(a), which #61 gives for s >= 1/2.
3. The Laves phases (#64): the big atom M0 sits IN layer k (studies/2026-11-12-laves-three-layer-swap). Is its piece symmetric under
   sigma_k at h layers, which would explain why it is fixed by layers k-1 and k only?
4. Rod groups: palindromic words (30 of 80 h layers here) make sigma_k a global mirror. Do the Hexagonality Law's coefficients have a
   reading as a count of global mirrors per period?
